headline: CORN DROPS 6%; HOGS RUN 18.7% TO CLOSE JULY
subheadline: Rain across the Belt knocked grains to multi-week lows Friday, while hogs had their biggest single-session gain in years and cattle quietly firmed.
lead: Corn closed Friday at $4.41, down 6% on the session, its worst day in months, as Belt rainfall eased yield fears and funds rotated hard out of grains. Hogs closed at $98.85, up 18.7%, a move that size demands attention regardless of what drove it. July ends with grains broken and livestock split: cattle patient, hogs running, milk in freefall.
the_takeaway: Grains broke on weather; watch whether funds come back or stay out.
teaser: Corn's worst day in months. Hogs' biggest day in years. July did not go quietly.

one_number.context: A move that size in lean hogs, closing at $98.85, is not a normal session. It dwarfs anything the hog complex has done this year and demands a catalyst explanation before Monday's open. Check the news; if there is no fundamental anchor, this is a position unwind or a reporting anomaly, not a demand story.

yesterdays_call.summary: Called corn lower through $4.41 Friday. Corn closed at $4.4075 -- right at the doorstep but did not print below the target level.
yesterdays_call.note: Miss by a tick. The directional read was correct -- corn broke hard on Belt rain, funds rotated out, and the session was the worst in months. But $4.4075 did not clear $4.41, so the level call did not play out. Own it and watch whether Monday continuation puts the market through that figure.

sections.title: Grains Break on Belt Rain
sections.body:
- Corn closed Friday at **$4.41**, down 6.0% on the session, as precipitation across the Corn Belt eased yield concerns during the critical dough-to-dent stage and funds rotated out hard with no weather story left to defend.
- Soybeans fell 1.8% to $11.72 nearby; wheat lost another 2.7% to $6.39, adding to Thursday's 2.9% break and leaving Chicago wheat down sharply for the week.
- The Dec '26 corn contract at $4.64 only dropped 1%, which says the new-crop market is pricing in a better harvest than nearby traders want to own right now.
sections.catalyst: Belt rainfall eases yield concerns during corn dough-to-dent stage; fund selling follows.
sections.bottom_line: Rain won the week. Until the Pro Farmer crop tour numbers land, there is no weather bid to buy.
sections.vs_yesterday: Corn: Thursday's soft close became Friday's hard break, 6% confirms the fund exit.

sections.title: Hogs Run Hard; Cattle Firm
sections.body:
- Lean hogs closed Friday at **$98.85**, up 18.7%, the kind of single-session move that either reflects a genuine fundamental shock or a position unwind so large it distorts the close; no clean fundamental headline in the news bucket explains the full magnitude.
- Live cattle firmed to $231.75, up 1.9%, with feeders adding 1.6% to $348.02, as the corn break reduced input costs and cash trade remained elusive per Friday reports.
- The Cargill Fort Morgan/Schuyler lockout, ongoing since May 19, continues to create processing-constrained dynamics rather than supply-constrained ones; no resolution announced.
sections.catalyst: Corn break reduces feeder cost pressure; hog move lacks clean fundamental anchor.
sections.bottom_line: Cattle are patient and methodical; hogs need a Monday explanation or Friday's print is noise.
sections.vs_yesterday: Cattle: held and firmed as called; hog move was not flagged and demands scrutiny.

sections.title: Crude Firms; Milk Breaks Hard
sections.body:
- WTI crude closed Friday at **$84.67**, up 2.8%, as Iran-Hormuz tensions, with the Strait of Hormuz premium that built since early April now deflating on diplomatic progress, still provided enough floor support to partially offset an 8% weekly loss in Brent.
- Saudi Arabia pushed a maritime coalition narrative late in the week, keeping a risk floor under oil even as China's Q2 crude imports declined on high prices from the Hormuz disruption.
- Class III Milk closed at $15.67, down 7.9% Friday, hitting the 34th percentile of its 52-week range; a Missouri rice farmer's fertilizer cost story ($300-$350 per ton more than 2025) is a reminder that input costs are not following commodity prices lower.
sections.catalyst: Saudis push maritime coalition; China Q2 crude imports fell on Hormuz-driven high prices; milk breaks without a specific weekly catalyst.
sections.bottom_line: Crude held its floor; milk did not. Input costs are moving independently of output prices.

sections.title: Policy and Trade: Farm Bill Moves
sections.body:
- Senate Ag Chairman Boozman released an updated farm bill draft Friday that permanently authorizes year-round E15 sales nationwide, a structural positive for corn demand that the futures market has not priced in yet.
- NGFA is pressing for USMCA renegotiation to address rail transportation delays into Mexico, a friction point that is quietly adding cost and uncertainty to grain export logistics.
- China's **$17 billion** annual US ag purchase commitment through 2028, announced May 18, has not translated into sustained futures support; the North Dakota State study estimate of $15 billion in active tariff costs continues to partially offset the headline number.
sections.catalyst: Boozman farm bill draft released Friday evening; NGFA USMCA grain logistics push.
sections.bottom_line: E15 permanence is real corn demand news; it needs a markup date before the market prices it.

outside_the_pit.title: Finland Detects First-Ever African Swine Fever Cases Near Russian Border
outside_the_pit.body: Finland confirmed ASF for the first time, near the Russian border. If it moves west into EU pork supply chains, it tightens global pork availability and puts a structural floor under US hog prices that has nothing to do with Friday's session move.

outside_the_pit.title: Farm Bill Draft Adds Year-Round E15, Revises SNAP Cost-Sharing
outside_the_pit.body: Boozman's updated draft makes year-round E15 permanent and restructures SNAP state cost-sharing. No markup date yet, but permanent E15 would add roughly 500 million bushels of annual corn demand if adopted. Watch for a committee date announcement.

the_more_you_know.title: Old Crop vs. New Crop: What the 23-Cent Corn Spread Is Telling You
the_more_you_know.body: Nearby corn closed at $4.41 while Dec '26 held $4.64, a 23-cent carry. That spread widening tells you the market expects the harvest to be large enough to rebuild stocks, but is not yet convinced nearby supply is tight. When carry widens during yield formation, it is the market pricing harvest pressure, not current demand. Watch whether that spread narrows on crop tour numbers.

watch_list.time: Week of Aug 3: Pro Farmer Crop Tour
watch_list.desc: Field-level yield estimates for corn and beans. Corn below 170 bu/acre national average revives the weather premium that Friday's rain killed. Above 175 confirms the break.
USDA Crop Progress. Corn condition rated good-to-excellent below 60% adds back some weather premium; above 65% and the market stays on the defensive.
Weekly Export Sales. Corn below 700K MT keeps funds on the sideline; beans below 300K MT says the China commitment is not translating into purchase orders.
Lean hogs need a fundamental explanation for Friday's 18.7% move. If no catalyst surfaces over the weekend, treat Friday's close as noise and watch for a corrective open.

daily_quote.text: It's tough to make predictions, especially about the future.
